newsitem.title: USA: Few antitrust problems seen for Hilton - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Few antitrust problems seen for Hilton - analysts.

text.p: Analysts saw few immediate antitrust problems Tuesday in Hilton Hotels Corp's proposed acquisition of ITT Corp, but they said it was too early to make a judgment.

"When it comes to a deal of this magnitude there is always a question" involving antitrust, said David Leibowitz, a managing director of Burnham Securities in New York. But he doubted there would be any serious problem.
Cautioning it was "a bit premature to be concerned about antitrust implications when we haven't even seen response to the bid" by Hilton, Leibowitz said he considered the match to be "a good fit."
For example, while both firms operate hotel/casinos in Las Vegas, he said, they are aimed at different audiences: ITT is at the top end of the spectrum and Hilton is more middle class.
Robert Skitol, a Washington lawyer with Drinker, Biddle and Reath, said that the government would compare the two hotel chains room-by-room, city-by-city.
"I doubt the overlap is competitively significant enough to give rise to antitrust concerns in major cities like New York or Los Angeles," he said.
"The chances are there are a handful of cities where there is a significant overlap. I can imagine they would want divestiture there."
Hilton Hotels Chief Executive Officer Stephen Bollenbach told Reuters on Monday that he believed there would be no problem in getting approval from federal antitrust regulators.

But attorney Steve Axxin, of Skadden and Arps in New York, agreed with Leibowitz that it was premature to make any statement about whether such a deal would win the approval of the government. He said that a complex and detailed analysis would have to be done before that question could be answered.
In addition, Axxin warned that state attorneys general might become interested, further slowing things.

Axxine said that if a state sees its economic interests threatened it would not hesitate to take its own action to stop a deal. Axxin cited a case in California in which the federal government approved a supermarket merger, only to have the state go to court and stop it.
